brief.head: Why religion exists
brief.text: Consolation, ex­pla­na­tion and cod­i­fi­ca­tion: Amit Varma of­fered three rea­sons re­li­gion ex­ists. {076-C04} Ajay Shah added that co­her­ent bands of 150 be­liev­ers won wars. {#bands}

brief.head: Seeker to columnist
brief.text: Raja Ram Mohan Roy began as a seeker, writ­ing in Persian, Amit Varma said. Writing later in Bengali, he be­came some­thing like a mod­ern colum­nist, out to per­suade. {076-S10}

brief.head: No cotton-wearers
brief.text: Worshipping Shiva or Vishnu once con­ferred no iden­tity, the his­to­rian Manu Devadevan ar­gues, any more than wear­ing cot­ton made any­one a “cot­ton wearer”. {076-C07}

brief.head: Freelance zeal
brief.text: The Industrial Revolution cre­ated the free­lance mis­sion­ary, Amit Varma said: any­one, even a shoe­maker, could go out, and jour­nals of their ac­counts sold in the hun­dreds of thou­sands. {076-S08}

brief.head: Prudes from abroad
brief.text: What passes for san­skari mod­esty, Amit Varma ar­gued, is a Victorian im­port. William Jones’s trans­la­tion drained the sen­su­al­ity from the orig­i­nal *Shakuntala*. {076-S09}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: What hap­pens when you write some­thing down is that it be­comes os­si­fied.
thought.who: Amit Varma, agreeing with Ajay Shah that an oral tradition stays malleable

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on a faith of many stories
lead.head: More Hinduisms than Hindus

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma in Episode 76

body: Amit Varma opened with a dis­claimer. He is a non-believer, he said, and has been for all his adult life. But Hinduism is “a river that runs through this space and through all of us”, and the sim­ple sto­ries told about it miss the point.

He named two. The first is na­tion­al­ist: a glo­ri­ous Hindu past, in­ter­rupted by for­eign in­vaders, that must be re­vived as a Hindu rash­tra. The sec­ond is aca­demic, and Varma said he held it until re­cently: Hinduism as a re­cent con­struc­tion, its name coined by a Britisher in the late 18th cen­tury, its Vedic ver­sion sold to the British by Brahmin in­ter­locu­tors.
Both, he ar­gued, are im­posed from the top. Following the his­to­rian Manu Pillai, he of­fered a third view: “the name may be new, but the river was al­ways there.” {076-C01}
Over the next hour and a quar­ter, with Ajay Shah ask­ing the ques­tions, he fol­lowed that river from the first hu­mans to the present.
## Mixed from the start

Modern hu­mans reached the sub­con­ti­nent be­tween 65,000 and 60,000 years ago, Varma said. Pastoralists from Iran set­tled at Mehrgarh about 7,000 years ago, and mi­grants from the steppes ar­rived around 2100 BCE, mostly men, who mixed with the lo­cals.
Genetics, he said, can now date such ar­rivals where ar­chae­ol­ogy could not. “Now we don’t know whether they in­vaded or not, but there cer­tainly was an Aryan mi­gra­tion.” {076-C02}
Even Sanskrit picked up sounds from lan­guages al­ready spo­ken here. “It it­self is a khichdi,” Varma said. {076-S01}

In the Puranic pe­riod that fol­lowed, Brahmins with­out the power to im­pose their be­liefs ab­sorbed local gods in­stead of eras­ing them. Varma called it “a cu­ra­tion driven by spon­ta­neous order”, a re­li­gion “form­ing it­self from the bot­tom up”. {076-C05}
Shah com­pared it to lan­guage, which shifts a lit­tle every hun­dred kilo­me­tres.
## Borders drawn

Invasions from the north gave feud­ing sects their first sense of a com­mon other. Colonialism sharp­ened it. Varma re­told Pillai’s image of four squab­bling brown-skinned men who feel united only when a white man at­tacks them all. {076-C09}
Europeans who could not grasp an open-source re­li­gion, Varma said, did what minds do with too much com­plex­ity: they made up a story, “which is pos­si­bly false”. {076-C10}
Indian re­sponses fol­lowed. Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s gen­teel Brahmo Samaj pleased the British; Dayanand Saraswati’s Arya Samaj out­lasted it. Bal Gangadhar Tilak took re­li­gion onto the streets.
Vinayak Savarkar then sup­plied a test of be­long­ing: India had to be both your home­land and your holy land. “Hinduism is a sub­set of Hindutva,” Varma said, sum­ming up Savarkar’s idea. {076-C11}
## What re­mains
Caste, Varma said, is a so­cial evil, like sati, and it has to go. He is scep­ti­cal of top-down fixes. His hope lies in mar­kets, where those who dis­crim­i­nate pay a price. {076-C12}

Shah pre­dicted that pros­per­ity would do its own work. Religiosity peaks in the mid­dle, he said, and India, after the 1991 re­forms, is there now. “In time sec­u­lar­i­sa­tion will come for India as well.” {076-C13}

Varma ended with an ap­peal to English-speaking urban elites: don’t be con­de­scend­ing. He used to think there were as many Hinduisms as there are Hindus. Now, he said, he thinks there are more. {076-J07}
Read his­tory, he urged, to un­der­stand how things came to be, while keep­ing your own val­ues in­tact. {076-C16}

second.label: The open-source epics
second.head: Bengal drew the line
second.deck: Amit Varma on the Ramayana as a river, rewritten across regions and centuries

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the open-source Ramayana

body: The Lakshman Rekha, today a metaphor for a line no one should cross, is not in Valmiki’s Ramayana. It first ap­pears, Amit Varma said, in Krittivasa’s Bengali ver­sion, from around the 15th cen­tury. {#rekha}

Drawing on AK Ramanujan’s essay *300 Ramayanas*, Varma called the epics open source, rewrit­ten at dif­fer­ent times and places ac­cord­ing to local cus­toms. {076-R17} Surpanakha is ugly in Valmiki and beau­ti­ful in Kamban. In the Telugu ver­sion, Urmila sleeps for four­teen years, half for her­self and half for Lakshman, so that he can stay awake.
Krittivasa also added the wash­er­man who starts the gos­sip about Sita. Varma was not dis­turbed that there is no one book; he finds it “ut­terly won­der­ful”. {076-S03}

quote.text: you never step into the same river twice, so you never step into the same Ramayana twice, and that’s amaz­ing.

third.head: Nothing to teach them

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the missionary who changed his mind

body: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg ar­rived with the usual mis­sion­ary im­pulse: con­vert these peo­ple. Then he en­gaged, Amit Varma said, and found much wis­dom in the later Vedas.

He wrote to his su­pe­ri­ors that they had got it wrong. “There is noth­ing we have to teach them,” he wrote, as Varma told it. “The best of our learn­ings are mir­rored some­where or the other in their teach­ings.” {076-S07}
His su­pe­ri­ors slapped him down. In ef­fect, Varma said, they ac­cused him of Stockholm syn­drome, “though of course the term didn’t exist then”. {076-J04}

Manu Pillai records many such re­spect­ful di­a­logues and de­bates, Varma said, but they were a small mi­nor­ity in a shrill dis­course, much as in­tel­li­gent dis­course is today. That age, he joked, also had its own Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, chat­ting civilly with British in­ter­locu­tors. {076-J05}

box.title: Varma’s primary source
box.text: It was his pri­mary source for the Puranic pe­riod, Amit Varma said: Manu Pillai’s *Gods, Guns and Missionaries*, whose in­tro­duc­tory essay, ‘A Brief History of Hinduism’, syn­the­sises it so beau­ti­fully that ev­ery­one should go out and buy the book. {#buybook}

sections.label: The deep past
sections.head: Nomads through a narrow pass
sections.caption: the long line that connects us all
body: Amit Varma began with a poem. In Dilip Chitre’s *Father Returning Home*, a tired fa­ther gets off the train “like a word dropped from a long sen­tence” and falls asleep “think­ing of no­mads en­ter­ing a sub­con­ti­nent through a nar­row pass.” {076-J08} That image, Varma said, is where he wanted to begin.

The first ev­i­dence of Homo sapi­ens, he said, is found in Africa 300,000 years ago. {#sapiens} The suc­cess­ful dis­per­sal out of Africa came about 70,000 years ago; ear­lier mi­grants left no trace in the ge­netic record.
Between 65,000 and 60,000 years ago, some reached the sub­con­ti­nent. Ajay Shah, cit­ing Tony Joseph’s *Early Indians*, traced their route along the coast from the gulf near Basra into Kutch.

About 7,000 years ago, pas­toral­ists from Iran set­tled at Mehrgarh and min­gled with the early Indians; then came the Harappan civil­i­sa­tion. From Devdutt Pattanaik’s new book on Harappa, Varma took a frame he loves: the city’s de­sign shows that it pri­ori­tised traders over raiders. {076-C03}
## Migration, not in­va­sion

Around 2100 BCE came mi­grants from the steppes, mostly men. Talk of an Aryan in­va­sion turned toxic, Varma said, partly be­cause the Nazis loved the story, and partly be­cause of a feel­ing that “we are the orig­i­nal peo­ple”.
Genetics, since Luca Cavalli-Sforza’s *The History and Geography of Human Genes*, can date such ar­rivals with sur­pris­ing cer­tainty. {076-R14}
~ The new­com­ers changed too. The Vedas, Varma said, are not one se­ries like *Harry Potter*: the early and later Vedas are star­tlingly dif­fer­ent. {076-J10}

quote.text: Ahimsa is not just non­vi­o­lence, but what is the ul­ti­mate sort of ex­pres­sion of it is ac­tu­ally peace­ful trade.

sections.label: The Puranic age
sections.head: Make the dude an avatar
sections.caption: how local gods joined the family
body: As Brahmins car­ry­ing the Vedic re­li­gion fanned out across the sub­con­ti­nent, Amit Varma said, they lacked the po­lit­i­cal power to im­pose their be­liefs. So they adapted, ab­sorb­ing local be­liefs and telling sto­ries about them. Those sto­ries be­came the Puranas.

In Andhra, a myth had Vishnu con­sort with a Chenchu woman, and their child be­came the Chenchu god. In Tamil coun­try, Ayyanar be­came Shiva’s son. Shaivites ex­panded Shiva’s fam­ily; Vaishnavites made a major local god an avatar. {076-S02}
Ajay Shah asked whether Hinduism stayed mal­leable be­cause it was vast, oral and older than the print­ing press. Varma agreed: writ­ing some­thing down os­si­fies it. {076-C06}
## Rubbing shoul­ders

The scholar MG Ranade said Hinduism in this pe­riod was con­quered by the mul­ti­tudes. In Dilip Menon’s de­scrip­tion, an­ces­tors, local he­roes, Vedic gods and na­ture gods “all rubbed shoul­ders in a seam­less fab­ric of wor­ship”. {076-J14}
It was no tran­quil fab­ric. Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists de­stroyed each other’s places of wor­ship; it was, Varma said, “ac­tu­ally like *Game of Thrones*”. {076-J09}

~ Brahmins them­selves var­ied: some veg­e­tar­ian, some not, some cre­mat­ing their dead, some bury­ing them. Hinduism, Varma said, formed from the bot­tom up, through the lives and rit­u­als of peo­ple. {076-C05}

quote.text: While for Vishnu, if you’re up against a major local god, just make the dude an avatar and you’re com­pletely fine there.

sections.label: Islam arrives
sections.head: The bandit who stayed
sections.caption: roving and stationary bandits
body: Islam first came to India not to in­vade but to trade, Amit Varma said, with peace­ful mer­chants on the Kerala coast; some say within Muhammad’s life­time. {#trade} That may be one rea­son com­mu­nal feel­ing can seem lower in the south.

The raiders came from the north, and they did de­stroy tem­ples. To ex­plain what fol­lowed, Varma turned to the econ­o­mist Mancur Olson. A rov­ing ban­dit takes what he can and leaves noth­ing stand­ing. A sta­tion­ary ban­dit stays, and “doesn’t want to kill the goose that will lay the golden eggs”. {076-C08}

So he gov­erns, fits in and be­comes of the peo­ple, as the Mughals did by mar­ry­ing Rajput princesses. Once rule set­tled, Varma said, cit­ing the his­to­rian Richard Eaton, vi­o­lence was con­fined to the edges. {076-J17}
## Mixing, and an other

Syncretism fol­lowed. In Sindh, Ali was adopted as an avatar of Vishnu. In bat­tles be­tween a Mughal em­peror and a Hindu rebel, Varma said, half the emperor’s gen­er­als were Hindu, and Turkish mer­ce­nar­ies fought for Shivaji, if he re­mem­bered cor­rectly. {076-S04}
Ajay Shah urged cau­tion about sin­gling out tales of cru­elty, since “there are no good guys in the me­dieval world”. People of that pe­riod, he said, should not be judged by today’s stan­dards.
~ Still, Varma said, for the first time there was a sense of an other to unite against. It would sharpen when colo­nial­ism began.

quote.text: you’ll find that half the gen­er­als of the Mughal Emperor were Hindu.

sections.label: The missionaries
sections.head: Ten thousand, or thirty-eight
sections.caption: colonial simplification
body: When some­thing is too com­plex to grasp, Amit Varma said, the mind craves clo­sure and makes up a story, pos­si­bly a false one. {076-C10} That is what Europeans did with an open-source re­li­gion they could not grok.
Missionaries sent back the most lurid tales they could. On sati, a real so­cial evil, one re­port claimed ten thou­sand in a sin­gle year. When Manu Pillai checked, the fig­ure was 38. {076-S06}

The ac­counts even ex­plained sati with an in­cen­tive story built on wrong as­sump­tions: men feared their sup­pos­edly un­faith­ful wives would kill them, so they made sure wid­ows burned with them. In parts of me­dieval Europe, Varma noted, un­faith­ful wives were burnt at the stake.
## Cutting the body to fit
Once the British began to gov­ern, they im­posed their own laws. In Purushottam Agrawal’s words, “in­stead of cut­ting the cloth to fit the body, they cut the body to fit the cloth.” {076-J15}

They took a Brahminical, caste-based view of Indian re­li­gion, ran a cen­sus in which ev­ery­one ticked a box, and pushed their story through schools. To give it­self a his­tory, Varma said, quot­ing Sudipta Kaviraj, is a community’s most fun­da­men­tal act of self-identification.
~ Unlike the early Brahmins, the colonis­ers wanted to rule, Varma said. Assimilation was no longer an op­tion, and a counter-story had to be built.

quote.text: Now thirty eight is still thirty eight too many, but you know, the num­bers are out of whack.

sections.label: Arriving at Hindutva
sections.head: Homeland and holy land
sections.caption: Savarkar’s test of belonging
body: From the re­form­ers, Amit Varma said, the line runs to mod­ern po­lit­i­cal Hinduism. His own he­roes are the Congress mod­er­ates, Ranade, Gokhale and Agarkar, “men who fol­low lib­eral ends through con­ser­va­tive means”. {076-J18}

Gokhale was al­ways fight­ing Bal Gangadhar Tilak, whom Varma finds odi­ous in many ways: he did not want girls ed­u­cated. But as a strate­gist he was deeply as­tute. He re­vived Shivaji as a brand and turned Ganapati, a local fes­ti­val, into a grand cel­e­bra­tion that brought hun­dreds of thou­sands onto the streets. {076-S12}
What Tilak never did was de­fine Hinduism. That fell to Vinayak Savarkar.
## A po­lit­i­cal mas­ter­stroke

Savarkar made Hindutva the um­brella and Hinduism one part of it. To be­long, India had to be both your home­land and your holy land. That oth­ered the British, and Muslims, who turn to Mecca, while bring­ing in Buddhists, Jains, Shaivites, Vaishnavites and Dalits. {076-C11}

Nobody asked why the line should fall there, Varma said; it sim­ply worked. Shruti Kapila had told him Hindutva is “a the­ory of vi­o­lence in search of a his­tory”. Savarkar gave it the his­tory. {076-J16}
~ It was, Varma ar­gued, a rad­i­cal de­par­ture: a tra­di­tion that had taken in the mul­ti­tudes was now built on hard­core oth­er­ing.

quote.text: He re­al­izes that if I want to build a po­lit­i­cal move­ment, we can’t talk about it in elite draw­ing rooms.

portraits.caption: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
portraits.credit: Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions

sections.label: Caste and today
sections.head: Ambedkar, meet Adam Smith
sections.caption: markets and the end of caste
body: Amit Varma took stock through caste. He often calls it Hinduism’s orig­i­nal sin, though it is not orig­i­nal as such. It is a so­cial evil, like sati, and it has to go.

He is scep­ti­cal of top-down fixes. Savarkar in­sisted Dalits be­longed and re­peat­edly held inter-caste feasts that an­gered Brahmins. The BJP was cred­ited with unit­ing the Hindu vote in 2014; in prac­tice it worked ex­ist­ing fis­sures like every party: non-Jatav Dalits in UP, non-Maratha OBCs in Maharashtra.

His hope lies in mar­kets. After 1991, hun­dreds of mil­lions came out of poverty, in­clud­ing hun­dreds of mil­lions of Dalits. The Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad once told him his he­roes were Ambedkar and Adam Smith. {076-S14}

Change will be slow, be­cause par­a­digms change one fu­neral at a time. But in a free mar­ket, dis­crim­i­na­tion has a price: “A rupee is a rupee, whether a Dalit is pay­ing you or a Brahmin is pay­ing you.” {076-C12}
## The peak in the mid­dle

Ajay Shah added a final force. The very poor are not es­pe­cially re­li­gious, he said, and sec­u­lar­i­sa­tion comes with wealth, ed­u­ca­tion and con­nec­tion to the world. The 1991 re­forms put India at the re­li­gious peak of the mid­dle. {076-C13}
~ The gen­teel Hinduism of Ram Mohan Roy, Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru seemed set­tled to Shah’s parents’ gen­er­a­tion. Varma said it was bound to fail: “They were de­ra­ci­nated elites.” {076-C14}

quote.text: to be a good Hindu is per­haps to just em­brace all of the world as it is and look at it with love.

art.caption: Amit Varma on markets and the end of caste

quote.text: If you want to un­der­stand your so­ci­ety, you have to un­der­stand the deep past. So just keep an open mind. Remember all of the things that you’re read­ing are de­scrip­tion, not pre­scrip­tion.

p3.title: Tellings and retellings
p3.deck: A mouse, an ox-god, two Savarkars and a curled tongue

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the night that made Dayanand Saraswati
stories.head: Of mice and the Arya Samaj
body: One night at a Shiva tem­ple, Dayanand Saraswati watched a mouse eat the prasad that had been left for the idol. As Amit Varma told it, he ex­pected the worst: “Oh my God, this is the idol of Shiva, the God will strike the mouse down dead.” {076-S11}
Instead, “noth­ing hap­pens, a mouse eats a prasad and goes away.” Dayanand began to ques­tion what he was see­ing. He trav­elled, and spent a few years with a her­mit.

He was, Varma said, a very cu­ri­ous man. Once, on the banks of the Ganga, he came across a corpse and cut it open: the scrip­tures had de­scribed what bod­ies look like in­side, and he wanted to see if it was true. It was not.
The British were not part of his scene at all. What dis­gusted him was the Puranic melange, the khichdi of ev­ery­thing. He wanted a purer faith rooted in the early Vedas, and founded the Arya Samaj.

Yet he learned from his ri­vals. At the Brahmo Samaj in Kolkata, he was told he could not speak in high­fa­lutin lan­guage; he had to speak the lan­guage of the peo­ple. {#hindi} So, Varma thinks, he began writ­ing in Hindi.
He picked up pam­phle­teer­ing, pub­lic­ity, mar­ket­ing and brand build­ing there too. But he was build­ing a dif­fer­ent, much more mil­i­tant kind of move­ment.

~ When Dayanand died, the elites as­sumed the Brahmo Samaj would thrive and the Arya Samaj would fall away. {#elites} The re­verse hap­pened. From the core of the Arya Samaj, Varma said, emerged mod­ern po­lit­i­cal Hinduism.
stories.why: A sin­gle fal­si­fy­ing ob­ser­va­tion can launch a move­ment. Dayanand’s elite rival taught him the pub­lic­ity that helped his move­ment out­last theirs. Real re­form, Varma said, comes from below, even if it goes in di­rec­tions he dis­likes. {076-C14}
stories.postscript: The Brahmo Samaj be­came al­most ir­rel­e­vant out­side the elite. The hosts’ dear friend Devangshu Datta is a Brahmo Samaji. {076-R21}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Dayanand Saraswati’s mouse

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the missionaries sent home
stories.head: The ox-god was made in Italy
body: Missionaries were not al­ways paid by the mer­chants, Amit Varma said. Like a mod­ern NGO rais­ing funds at home, they told the most ex­treme ver­sion of every story. {076-S05}
One Italian mis­sion­ary in­vented a god, half man and half ox, who de­manded the blood of 400 vir­gins; Indian par­ents, in this tale, gave up chil­dren to be be­headed. {#oxgod}

Other tales were erotic. Lonely wid­ows at the shrine of Akbar’s grand­son took their pick of male pil­grims. Powerful women ran gangs that kid­napped men for a night, and one woman found her cap­tive was “her own law­fully wed­ded hus­band”. {076-J02}

~ Europe, Varma con­cluded, “must have been deeply sex­u­ally re­pressed”. {076-J03} Voltaire read such sto­ries and called India bar­barous; James Mill wrote his his­tory of India with­out vis­it­ing.
stories.why: Who pays for knowl­edge shapes what it says. A fundrais­ing in­cen­tive turned re­ports on India into tabloid fic­tion, and Europe’s great thinkers built their pic­ture of the coun­try on it.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the missionaries’ tabloid tales

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the man before and after the Andamans
stories.head: Revolutionary in, radical out
body: Amit Varma has read pretty much every bi­og­ra­phy of Vinayak Savarkar, and he sees two men. “There is a Savarkar till 1910, and there is a Savarkar that comes later.” {076-S13}

Until 1910, Savarkar was a Bhagat Singh kind of fig­ure, Varma said, or­gan­is­ing rev­o­lu­tion­ary acts. Nehru praised his book; he shared a stage in London with Gandhi; Hindus and Muslims, he said, must throw off the yoke to­gether.

Then he was im­pris­oned in the Andamans, treated not as a po­lit­i­cal pris­oner but as a ter­ror­ist. {#andamans} Between the British jail­ers and the pris­on­ers stood mostly Pathan guards who bru­talised the in­mates; there are ru­mours of worse than tor­ture.
~ He came out close to 1920 rad­i­calised, hat­ing Muslims with a zeal, and wrote *Essentials of Hindutva*.

quote.text: if he died in nine­teen ten, we would think of him as we do of Bhagat Singh

stories.postscript: Varma has dis­cussed Savarkar in de­tail with Manu Pillai on *The Seen and the Unseen*, and sug­gests lis­ten­ing to that.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the two Savarkars

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what Sanskrit picked up from the locals
stories.head: Mothers had the last word
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah to say two words. In the first, the tongue hits the upper teeth: a den­tal sound, com­mon across the Indo-Aryan lan­guages. In the sec­ond, it curls back: a retroflex sound, ab­sent from those but present in all the Dravidian lan­guages.

Sanskrit, ar­riv­ing here, had picked these sounds up from the lan­guages al­ready spo­ken, Varma said. The point comes from Peggy Mohan’s *Wanderers, Kings, Merchants*, which cites Madhav Deshpande’s 1976 essay on the Rig Veda. {076-S01}

That essay “pretty much blew ev­ery­one away”, Varma said, be­cause Sanskrit had been seen as pure. He had been taught that all Indian lan­guages came from Sanskrit; that, he said, is ab­so­lutely not true.
~ Mohan’s ex­pla­na­tion is that the mi­grants were mostly men who mar­ried local women. The chil­dren grew up with their moth­ers for their first two or three years. {#mothers}
stories.why: Even the purest sa­cred lan­guage is a mix­ture. One small fact about sounds un­does both the story of a pure ori­gin and the story that Sanskrit is the mother of all Indian lan­guages.

overheard.who: Amit Varma, on the Bengali origins of the Lakshman Rekha

quiz.q: How did Shaivites and Vaishnavites absorb a major local god into their traditions?
quiz.a: Shaivites ex­panded Shiva’s fam­ily; Vaishnavites made the god an avatar of Vishnu.

quiz.q: In which version of the Ramayana does the Lakshman Rekha first appear?
quiz.a: Krittivasa’s Bengali Ramayana, from around the 15th cen­tury, not Valmiki’s orig­i­nal.

quiz.q: What two conditions did Savarkar set for belonging to Hindutva?
quiz.a: India must be both your home­land and your holy land.

quiz.q: What did Dayanand Saraswati see at a Shiva temple that set him questioning?
quiz.a: A mouse ate the prasad left for the idol, and noth­ing hap­pened.

quiz.q: In Mancur Olson’s frame, why does a stationary bandit govern rather than destroy?
quiz.a: He wants steady rev­enue, so he won’t kill the goose that lays golden eggs.

quiz.q: Which two heroes did the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad name to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Ambedkar and Adam Smith: one shows how deep the prob­lem is, the other the way out.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 76. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar (User:Jayantanth, public domain); Manu S. Pillai (Innocentbunny, CC BY-SA 4.0); Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain).

shelf.title: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
shelf.creator: Manu Pillai
shelf.why: Manu Pillai shows how fluid Hinduism was for cen­turies and how a shared Hindu iden­tity formed grad­u­ally, first against Islam and then against the British and their mis­sion­ar­ies.

shelf.title: The Forces That Shaped Hinduism (Episode 405 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Manu Pillai
shelf.why: The fuller ver­sion of this story, es­pe­cially on Savarkar.

shelf.title: Devdutt Pattanaik and the Stories That Shape Us (Episode 404 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Devdutt Pattanaik
shelf.why: A deep im­mer­sion in Indian mythol­ogy.

shelf.title: Arshia Sattar and the Complex Search for Dharma (Episode 315 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Arshia Sattar
shelf.why: Background for the episode’s ar­gu­ment that the epics are open-source rivers rather than fixed texts.

shelf.title: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
shelf.creator: Akshaya Mukul
shelf.why: Mukul’s mas­ter­piece shows how deeply Hindu na­tion­al­ist ideas ran through Indian so­ci­ety over the decades: the com­mu­nal strain was there all along, sec­u­lar lib­er­als were the fringe, and pol­i­tics sim­ply caught up with so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
shelf.why: The con­ver­sa­tional com­pan­ion to Akshaya Mukul’s book on how the Gita Press, through cul­ture and re­li­gion, fed mod­ern po­lit­i­cal Hinduism.

shelf.title: Early Indians
shelf.creator: Tony Joseph
shelf.why: Tony Joseph uses the genes of liv­ing peo­ple to re­con­struct thou­sands of years of Indian his­tory: the first Indians, the Harappans, the Aryan mi­gra­tion, and how caste en­dogamy set in about 2,000 years ago after mil­len­nia of in­ter­min­gling.

shelf.title: Tony Joseph’s episode on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Tony Joseph on the ge­netic his­tory of the sub­con­ti­nent, the audio com­pan­ion to Early Indians, in­clud­ing how India’s mi­grant groups mixed for thou­sands of years be­fore en­dogamy locked in.

shelf.title: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: The Story of India through Its Languages
shelf.creator: Peggy Mohan
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan reads India’s past through its liv­ing lan­guages, doing with lan­guage what Reich and Joseph did with genes: mi­grat­ing men mar­ried local women, so chil­dren spoke their mothers’ tongue first, and Sanskrit ab­sorbed local sounds such as retroflexes.

shelf.title: Understanding India Through Its Languages (Episode 232 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan’s lin­guis­tic his­tory of India in con­ver­sa­tion, the com­pan­ion to her book Wanderers, Kings, Merchants.

shelf.title: Who We Are and How We Got Here
shelf.creator: David Reich
shelf.why: Reich ex­plains how full-genome stud­ies re­con­struct human his­tory and over­turned re­ceived wis­dom from ar­chae­ol­ogy.

shelf.title: Father Returning Home
shelf.creator: Dilip Chitre
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite poems, whose phrase ‘man’s es­trange­ment from a man-made world’ and clos­ing image of ‘no­mads en­ter­ing a sub­con­ti­nent through a nar­row pass’ have stayed with him.

shelf.title: Ahimsa: 100 Reflections on the Harappan Civilization
shelf.creator: Devdutt Pattanaik
shelf.why: Offers a frame Amit loves: Harappan cities pri­ori­tised traders over raiders, and ahimsa is vol­un­tary ex­change be­tween con­sent­ing adults.

shelf.title: The History and Geography of Human Genes
shelf.creator: Luca Cavalli-Sforza
shelf.why: Showed that ge­netic ev­i­dence can re­veal, with sur­pris­ing cer­tainty, when peo­ple ar­rived some­where and who they mixed with.

shelf.title: Genesis of Rgvedic Retroflexion
shelf.creator: Madhav Deshpande
shelf.why: A 1976 essay that ‘pretty much blew ev­ery­one away’ by show­ing that the Rig Veda’s lan­guage was in­flu­enced by what was spo­ken here be­fore.

shelf.title: A Prehistory of Hinduism
shelf.creator: Manu Devadevan
shelf.why: Argues that wor­ship­ping Shiva or Vishnu was sim­ply part of ev­ery­day life and not a marker of iden­tity.

shelf.title: 300 Ramayanas
shelf.creator: AK Ramanujan
shelf.why: Ramanujan’s essay shows the Ramayana con­stantly re­told across times and places, each ver­sion (tribal ones com­pletely dif­fer­ent) adapt­ing the epic to the so­ci­ety that told it.

shelf.title: Rebel Sultans
shelf.creator: Manu Pillai
shelf.why: Elaborates on the cul­tural mix­ing of the pe­riod, such as Hindu gen­er­als serv­ing Mughal em­per­ors and Muslim mer­ce­nar­ies fight­ing on the other side.

shelf.title: The Ivory Throne
shelf.creator: Manu Pillai
shelf.why: Documents that it was once com­mon for women in Kerala to be bare-breasted, be­fore British prud­ery changed things.

shelf.title: Swapna Liddle and the Many Shades of Delhi (Episode 367 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Swapna Liddle
shelf.why: Historian Swapna Liddle on Delhi: Delhi College, po­etry in the city’s news­pa­pers and mushaira news­let­ters, and how the British used ed­u­ca­tion to push their nar­ra­tives about Indian his­tory.

shelf.title: Devangshu Datta Traded His Corduroy Pants (Episode 348 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Devangshu Datta
shelf.why: A life-and-times con­ver­sa­tion with the hosts’ friend Devangshu Datta, from chess and his Brahmo Samaj back­ground to a fam­ily tree with three great-grandfathers who had in­sti­tu­tions named after them and a fourth who was a river pi­rate in Bengal.

shelf.title: Vinayak Calling Vinayak (Episode 385 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vinayak Chaturvedi
shelf.why: A fur­ther deep dive for any­one in­trigued by the ‘two Savarkars’.

shelf.title: The Ferment of Our Founders (Episode 272 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
shelf.why: Shruti Kapila on the fer­ment of India’s founders, the source of her line that Hindutva is ‘a the­ory of vi­o­lence in search of a history’.

shelf.title: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
shelf.why: The Dalit thinker whose two he­roes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, a pair­ing cen­tral to Amit’s hope for end­ing caste.

laughs.text: One of the missionaries’ in­vented tales was about women who ran gangs that kid­napped men off the street for a night. In it, a woman has a man kid­napped ‘only to find out it is her own law­fully wed­ded hus­band.’

Judging by the sto­ries mis­sion­ar­ies sent home, Amit con­cludes that ‘Europe at this point must have been deeply sex­u­ally repressed’, and calls these tales ‘a mad fan­tasy of some bored, frus­trated mis­sion­ary some­where.’

Ziegenbalg’s su­pe­ri­ors re­spond to his praise of Indian wis­dom with, in ef­fect, ‘fuck off, what are you doing?’ Amit says they were ac­cus­ing him of Stockholm syn­drome, ‘though of course the term didn’t exist then.’

On how small the space for civil dis­course was in colo­nial times: ‘some­where that age also has an Amit Varma and Ajay Shah and they’re chat­ting with the British in­ter­locu­tors and ev­ery­thing is civil. But that’s a small part of it.’
On how in­va­sion united feud­ing sects: ‘a com­mon enemy comes who says, Stop this show, you’re all going to jail. Right? And in­stantly we unite against that com­mon enemy.’
Amit raises his own line: ‘I used to think there are as many Hinduisms as there are Hindus. I ac­tu­ally think there are more Hinduisms than there are Hindus.’

Amit opens with Dilip Chitre’s poem ‘Father Returning Home’. In it, a tired fa­ther gets off the train ‘like a word dropped from a long sentence’ and falls asleep ‘think­ing of no­mads en­ter­ing a sub­con­ti­nent through a nar­row pass.’
Game of Thrones: Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists de­stroy­ing each other’s places of wor­ship is ‘ac­tu­ally like Game of Thrones, that peo­ple are just going mad.’
MG Ranade said that in the Puranic pe­riod Hinduism ‘was con­quered by the multitudes’, mean­ing it not only con­tains mul­ti­tudes but was made by them.
Dilip Menon, on Puranic syn­cretism: ‘de­ceased an­ces­tors, local he­roes and hero­ines, gods of the Vedic pan­theon and na­ture gods all rubbed shoul­ders in a seam­less fab­ric of wor­ship.’
Purushottam Agrawal on colo­nial law: ‘in­stead of cut­ting the cloth to fit the body, they cut the body to fit the cloth.’
Shruti Kapila: Hindutva is ‘a the­ory of vi­o­lence in search of a history’. Savarkar sup­plied the his­tory.
Richard Eaton ‘has writ­ten won­der­fully well’ about how, once the Mughal em­pire set­tled, vi­o­lence was con­fined to its ex­pand­ing edges.

Amit’s he­roes among the Congress mod­er­ates are Ranade, Gokhale and Agarkar, ‘men who fol­low lib­eral ends through con­ser­va­tive means’ and who didn’t want to burn ev­ery­thing down. They were set against ex­trem­ists like Tilak.
